DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
This proposal would raise the weekend room rate from £145 to £165 and require a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday. It projects at least £204,000 a year in extra room revenue.

The underlying case is reasonable: Harbourside is clearly priced below competitors, and £165 only brings it level with the cheapest of them. But the revenue figure uses the wrong room count and applies the higher rate to rooms that don't pay it. The evidence that guests aren't price-sensitive is really a seasonal effect. And the two-night minimum conflicts with the hotel's own wedding trade. The £204,000 is a ceiling, not the floor the proposal calls it.

## 1. Revenue errors

**The hotel has 112 rooms, not 124.** §2 says 112; §5 uses 124.
- 124 × 104 nights × 79% × £20 = **£203,800** (the arithmetic is correct)
- 112 × 104 nights × 79% × £20 = **£184,000**

**Not every room sells at the Best Available Rate (BAR).** The £20 rise applies only to rooms sold at BAR. §6 rightly protects contracted corporate rates and group rates, but §5 still counts those rooms. Wedding blocks alone are **38% of Saturday bookings**. If, say, 60% of weekend room-nights are sold at BAR, the uplift is about **£110,000**.

**Other deductions.** If BAR includes VAT, as UK hotel rates normally do, the £20 is £16.67 of net revenue. Rooms booked through online travel agencies also lose 15–20% of each extra £20 to commission.

The realistic figure is probably **around £90,000–110,000 a year**, before any loss of bookings. The exact number depends on what share of weekend rooms is sold at BAR, which the revenue team can get from its booking system.

## 2. The June–July 2025 "test" doesn't show price insensitivity

- **July is always busier.** Weekend occupancy rose from 81% in June to 89% in July. The proposal's own text says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The rise is what the season would produce at any price.
- **Most July bookings were probably made before the rate changed.** The rate went up in the last week of June. Many July weekend stays would already have been booked at £135, so July occupancy mostly reflects the old rate.
- **This rise is twice as large.** Last year's change was £10 (+7%); this one is £20 (+14%).
- **A better test** would compare July–September 2025 (at £145) with July–September 2024 (at £135), using bookings made after the change.

**The value-for-money score of 8.4** was given by guests paying £20–35 less than competitors charge. Raising prices will probably lower it, so it can't be used as evidence that prices can rise without cost.

The author's description repeats both arguments.

## 3. The two-night minimum is likely to lose revenue as designed

- **Wedding guests conflict with it directly.** They make up 38% of Saturday bookings and typically stay one night, Saturday only. If the minimum applies to them, wedding couples may move their room blocks to another hotel. If wedding guests are exempt, which seems likely given the group-rate protection, the minimum covers far fewer bookings than the proposal implies.
- **On quiet Saturdays it turns guests away.** The hotel sold out on 31 Saturdays. On the other 21, a guest who wants one night will book elsewhere rather than pay for two. That loses a room that would otherwise have sold.
- **So it isn't free extra revenue.** The proposal treats the minimum as pure upside and the £204,000 as a floor. In fact the minimum could add revenue on sold-out dates and lose it on the rest.

Hotels usually apply minimum stays only on dates expected to sell out (festival weekends, peak summer) and lift them when demand is weaker. The proposal should do the same.

## 4. Monitoring

- **The review trigger may react late.** It compares monthly occupancy with 2025. Because guests book weeks ahead, the effect of the new rate shows up in occupancy only gradually, and the strong July–August months will hide weakness at first. The weekly booking-pace review is the more useful early warning, so it should have its own trigger, for example new bookings for upcoming weekends running X% behind the same weeks in 2025.
- **The rate rise can absorb more lost bookings than the 5-point trigger suggests.** At £165, rooms sold at BAR could fall by about **12%** before revenue drops below today's level, around 9–10 occupancy points. That's a fairly comfortable buffer, which the proposal could have used as an argument in its favour.

## 5. What the evidence supports

- **The rate rise:** yes. The gap to competitors is real, £165 matches only the lowest of them, and the rise can absorb a meaningful loss of bookings before costing money.
- **The two-night minimum:** only on dates expected to sell out, with wedding blocks handled explicitly.

## Suggested changes before approval

1. Use 112 rooms, apply the £20 only to rooms sold at BAR, and state whether the figures include VAT and agency commission.
2. Replace the June-to-July comparison with a same-months-last-year comparison, or drop the claim that guests aren't price-sensitive.
3. Restrict the two-night minimum to dates expected to sell out, and set out how wedding blocks will be handled.
4. Show the revenue estimate as a range: a base case, plus a case where weekend occupancy falls by 5 points.
5. Add a trigger based on weekly booking pace, alongside the monthly occupancy check.

With these changes, the proposal would still support a rate rise, with a more accurate estimate of around £100,000 a year.
